explanations: terra: Those who يَقْطَعُونَ مَا أَمَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ أَن يُوصَلَ enact the severing that the source gloss says the Lord did not do.
terra: The garden fall likewise ends with فِي الْأَرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمَتَاعٌ إِلَىٰ حِينٍ, a bounded replacement dwelling after removal.

luna: The section’s dictionary form for ر ب ب includes a cloud that persists; here God shades the Israelites with cloud and sends food, so the enduring sky-cover is part of care in their wilderness. | terra: The cloud shades Israel while manna and quails are sent, joining the source dictionary's cloud image to sustained shelter and provision.
luna: The section glosses the orphan’s name through neglected care; this covenant expressly commands kindness to orphans, placing them among those owed good treatment.
terra: فَاذْكُرُونِي أَذْكُرْكُمْ gives remembrance as a reciprocal divine-human relation, the positive counterpart to being forgotten or left out.
terra: The cloud held under command between heaven and earth presents the source dictionary's cloud object as suspended and sustained within divine ordering.
luna: The section’s orphan is a vulnerable person taken in; this description of righteousness includes giving wealth to orphans, a concrete form of care.
terra: Allah says فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ and answers the caller, a direct statement of responsive nearness that rules out inattentive distance.

luna: The section’s dictionary form توديع الثوب means putting a garment in a case that preserves it; this verse uses clothing as a mutual covering between spouses, making protection a human relation as well as safekeeping. | terra: Spouses are called garments for one another, making covering and intimate mutual shelter a relational use of the garment image.
luna: The section’s image pairs need with provision; this answer about spending names orphans among those for whom good wealth is spent.

luna: The section glosses the orphan’s name through neglect of his good; this verse says reforming orphans’ affairs is best (“إِصْلَاحٌ لَّهُمْ خَيْرٌ”), making attentive care the stated response. | terra: Reform of orphans' affairs is called best and living together makes them brothers, replacing distance and neglected care with a household relation.

luna: The section separates a farewell from a lasting abandonment; in a divorce context, this verse says not to forget generosity between people even when they part, showing care can survive separation.
terra: The Ark contains tranquility from the Lord and a remnant مِمَّا تَرَكَ آلُ مُوسَىٰ وَآلُ هَارُونَ; what a family leaves is borne and preserved rather than discarded.
luna: The section’s need-to-provision image is sharpened by this contrast: Satan threatens poverty, while God promises forgiveness and bounty, so fear of need does not define what follows.
luna: The section gives need a place in the image of divine provision; this verse describes poor people who cannot travel to earn and do not beg insistently, making their need easy to overlook.

luna: The section’s dictionary form استودعته means entrusting a deposit for safekeeping; this verse says that when one person trusts another with a deposit, the trustee must return it, giving the keeping sense a human duty. | terra: فَإِنْ أَمِنَ بَعْضُكُم بَعْضًا فَلْيُؤَدِّ الَّذِي اؤْتُمِنَ أَمَانَتَهُ describes a deposit entrusted to another and the keeper's duty to return it.
terra: Mary is accepted, caused to grow well, and placed in Zakaria's care; recurring provision in her sanctuary shows a child entrusted to both human and divine keeping.
terra: The casting of pens decides أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ, making the choice of a guardian for the young Mary the ayah's central act.
terra: At Uhud the believers climb away without looking back while the Messenger calls from behind, staging human companions leaving the Prophet in danger.
terra: إِن يَنصُرْكُمُ اللَّهُ فَلَا غَالِبَ لَكُمْ is set against the explicit counterfactual وَإِن يَخْذُلْكُمْ; it names divine forsaking only to show that no other support could replace Him.
terra: When people warn believers that forces have gathered, they answer حَسْبُنَا اللَّهُ وَنِعْمَ الْوَكِيلُ, placing threatened lives in the best Trustee's care.

luna: The section says the Lord did not abandon the Prophet; this verse says God will not let any worker’s effort be lost and names people expelled from their homes for His cause among those promised reward. | terra: Allah promises not to let any worker's work be lost and immediately includes those who emigrated and were expelled from their homes, preserving both persons and deeds through forced departure.

luna: The section’s orphan is someone whose care can be neglected; this command forbids consuming the orphans’ property or exchanging their good for bad, giving neglect a concrete material form. | terra: Giving orphans their property back and not consuming it with one's own defines the faithful handling of what belongs to a vulnerable ward.

luna: The section links the orphan with vulnerable care that can be withheld; this verse warns against injustice to orphan girls in marriage, making fairness to them a specific form of not neglecting them. | terra: Fear of failing justice toward orphan girls governs the marriage instruction, exposing how guardianship can become exploitation rather than protection.

luna: The section connects the orphan with being taken in; this verse describes guardians testing orphans until maturity and then handing their property over, so care reaches the point of independence. | terra: Guardians test orphans until maturity and then deliver their property to them, turning temporary custody into faithful preservation rather than appropriation.
luna: The section’s orphan is one whose care can be neglected; this inheritance rule directs witnesses to give orphans and the poor something from the distribution and speak kindly to them.
terra: Those who fear leaving weak offspring behind are told to act justly, directly naming the anxiety that departure will expose dependent children.

luna: The section’s shelter and provision for the orphan are reversed by this warning: those who consume orphan property unjustly are consuming fire, a stark boundary against exploitation. | terra: Those who consume orphan property turn a protected charge into self-enrichment, the betrayal opposite to sheltering one whose care is easily neglected.
luna: The section connects sheltering an orphan to not neglecting his kindness; this command places orphans among neighbors to whom good treatment is owed.

luna: The section’s dictionary form وديعة is something left with another to preserve; this command to return trusts to their owners states the corresponding obligation of faithful keeping. | terra: Allah commands that trusts be rendered to their owners, stating the obligation created when something is left in another's keeping.
terra: The oppressed ask their Lord to bring them out of a tyrannical town and appoint a protector and helper, joining needed departure to requested divine guardianship.

luna: The section brings together departure, taking refuge, and enrichment; this verse promises that one who emigrates for God will find many places of refuge and ample provision on earth. | terra: One who leaves home migrating finds many places of refuge and abundance, and even death on the road leaves the reward secured with Allah.

luna: The section explains the orphan as one whose good may be neglected; this verse names orphan girls whose prescribed rights are not given, directly exposing the withholding of care and justice. | terra: The ayah addresses orphan women denied what was prescribed for them, a specific institutional form of the neglected care evoked by يَتِيم.

luna: The section examines what it means to leave someone; this verse forbids a husband from leaving a wife “as if suspended” (“كَالْمُعَلَّقَةِ”), naming the vulnerable in-between state that non-abandonment rules out.
terra: وَإِن يَتَفَرَّقَا يُغْنِ اللَّهُ كُلًّا makes separation itself the setting in which Allah enriches both parties, meeting the section's departure and sufficiency in one claim.

luna: The section glosses سجا with the dictionary form سكن (become still); this verse speaks of what “سَكَنَ فِي اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ,” linking the same settling sense to night and day under God’s care.
terra: وَلَا تَطْرُدِ الَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُم forbids the Prophet to drive away vulnerable worshippers, using the very expulsion action named in the source explanation of قَلَىٰ.
terra: Humans return to Allah alone and leave behind everything He had bestowed, sharply distinguishing the departing person from possessions that cannot accompany or keep them.

luna: The section glosses سجا with the dictionary forms سكن ودام (became still and lasted); this verse calls night “سَكَنًا,” a direct formulation of the quiet night before the reassurance. | terra: The breaker of dawn makes night سَكَنًا, directly pairing morning's emergence with the night's repose behind the section's oath.

luna: The section’s dictionary form استودعته means a deposit entrusted for protection; this verse names “مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمُسْتَوْدَعٌ” in human creation, placing settlement and safekeeping together. | terra: مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمُسْتَوْدَعٌ applies the section's deposit-and-abode pair to human generation from one soul.

luna: The section connects the orphan with protection rather than neglect; this command forbids approaching orphan property except in the best manner, stating a boundary on the guardian’s conduct. | terra: The command not to approach orphan property except in the best way until maturity treats it as a protected deposit.
terra: After expulsion from the garden, earth is made a settlement and provision for a time, combining forced departure with a temporary abode.

luna: The section’s dictionary image is a garment put in a case that preserves it; this verse says God provides clothing that covers nakedness and adorns people, connecting the garment to protection. | terra: Clothing is given to cover nakedness and as adornment, stating the garment's protective-covering function before 7:27 stages its loss.
terra: Satan strips Adam and his wife of their clothing to expose them, reversing the source dictionary's garment safely enclosed and the Qur'anic garment that covers.

luna: The section quotes the claim that the Lord is not forgetful; this verse says people forgot the meeting of this day and so are forgotten, making human neglect the boundary to the reassurance. | terra: فَالْيَوْمَ نَنسَاهُمْ is judicial abandonment in response to their forgetting the meeting, contrasting with 19:64's denial that the Lord is cognitively forgetful.
terra: Winds carry a heavy cloud and Allah drives it to dead land, so the cloud moves away yet its movement becomes delivery of life rather than expulsion.
terra: Lot's people answer his warning by demanding that his household be expelled from the town, staging communal rejection as literal removal.
terra: Allah saves Lot and his household except his wife, answering the expulsion threat in 7:82 with selective divine rescue.

luna: The section’s second departure image is active expulsion; Shuaib’s people threaten to drive him and the believers from their town unless they return to their religion, a human rejection contrasted with divine care. | terra: The arrogant chiefs threaten to expel Shuayb and the believers unless they return to the old religion, a messenger-specific repetition of forced separation.

luna: The section’s dictionary form غني القوم في دارهم means they stayed in their home; after Shuaib’s people are destroyed, this verse says it is as if they had never lived there (“كَأَنْ لَمْ يَغْنَوْا فِيهَا”). | terra: كَأَن لَّمْ يَغْنَوْا فِيهَا uses غ ن ي in the source dictionary's dwelling sense: the destroyed deniers are as though they had never remained in their homes.

luna: The section names a cloud that continues as a secondary dictionary sense; this verse again describes cloud shade over the Israelites alongside manna and quail, showing sustained provision in the wilderness. | terra: Allah shades the tribes with cloud and sends manna and quails, again making a cloud an enduring cover linked to care.
terra: Allah tells the angels that He is with them and commands them to make the believers firm in battle, converting divine presence into concrete support.

luna: The section’s sheltering of the orphan reverses vulnerability; this verse recalls the believers’ fear of being seized, then says God sheltered them (“فَآوَاكُمْ”), strengthened them, and provided good things. | terra: فَآوَاكُمْ says Allah sheltered a small, vulnerable community that feared being snatched away, then strengthened and provided for it.

luna: The section’s dictionary form وديعة is something left with another to safeguard; this verse forbids betraying trusts, stating the danger that the section’s safekeeping sense is meant to prevent. | terra: The ban on betraying trusts marks the moral opposite of receiving something for faithful safekeeping.

luna: The section rejects the idea that God has driven the Prophet away; this verse recalls people plotting to restrain, kill, or expel him, while God counters their plan. | terra: The plot to confine, kill, or expel the Prophet is set against Allah's counter-plan, showing human attempts to remove him held within divine governance.
terra: If the hearers turn away, they are reminded that Allah is their protector and the best protector and helper.
luna: The section pairs need with provision and develops care for the orphan; this rule assigns orphans a share of spoils, giving material support a concrete institutional form.
luna: The section glosses فآوى as joining someone; this verse says God joined the believers’ hearts, making their closeness itself a kind of refuge that human wealth could not create.
terra: يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ حَسْبُكَ اللَّهُ tells the Prophet that Allah is sufficient for him and joins believing followers to that support.

luna: The section’s dictionary form آوى includes joining and sheltering; here the emigrants “أَوَوْا وَنَصَرُوا” those who came to them, making refuge a human practice of support. | terra: The emigrants who left homes and the believers who sheltered and helped them are made mutual protectors, turning departure into received communal care.
terra: Those who believed and emigrated are again joined to those who sheltered and helped, and are named the true believers with provision assured.
terra: A person seeking protection must be granted refuge and then conveyed to a place of safety, defining shelter as custody that ends in secure delivery.
terra: The hostile people are recalled as having resolved to expel the Messenger, another specific attempt to force the Prophet away.
terra: At Hunayn the believers' numbers do not avail them and they turn away, creating the abandonment-like battlefield reversal answered in 9:26.
terra: Allah then sends tranquility upon His Messenger and believers and unseen forces, restoring support after the flight in 9:25.

luna: The section names عائلًا for need and فأغنى for its answer; this verse pairs fear of “عَيْلَةً” (poverty) with God enriching people from His bounty (“يُغْنِكُمُ اللَّهُ”). | terra: The only other عَيْلَة names feared poverty and immediately promises فَسَوْفَ يُغْنِيكُمُ اللَّهُ, bringing the section's ع ي ل and غ ن ي words together as need reversed by divine sufficiency.

luna: The section’s claim that the Lord did not leave the Prophet meets the cave scene: when his companion grieves, he says God is with them (“إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَنَا”), and God sends tranquility. | terra: When the Prophet has been expelled and is one of two in the cave, لَا تَحْزَنْ إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَنَا and the descending tranquility stage divine companionship at the sharpest human leaving.

luna: The section quotes the claim that the Lord is not forgetful; this verse says hypocrites forgot God and so were forgotten, a stated boundary that reverses the section’s assurance. | terra: نَسُوا اللَّهَ فَنَسِيَهُمْ presents reciprocal punitive abandonment of hypocrites, defining a judgment boundary rather than ordinary forgetfulness.
terra: The ayah recalls that Allah and His Messenger enriched the people from divine bounty, another direct use of غ ن ي for granted sufficiency.

luna: The section’s denied abandonment meets the three whose isolation made the earth seem constricted and who found no refuge except to God (“لَا مَلْجَأَ مِنَ اللَّهِ إِلَّا إِلَيْهِ”); the verse then says He turned toward them. | terra: The three “left behind” find no refuge from Allah except in Him; His turning toward them converts social and inward estrangement into restored relation.

luna: The section’s dictionary form غني القوم في دارهم is explicitly glossed as people dwelling in their home; this parable says the vegetation is gone as if it had never flourished (“كَأَنْ لَمْ تَغْنَ بِالْأَمْسِ”), reversing persistence into sudden disappearance. | terra: كَأَن لَّمْ تَغْنَ بِالْأَمْسِ likens worldly growth cut down overnight to something that had not flourished or remained the day before.

luna: The section’s gloss for the night is stillness and duration; this verse says night was made so people may rest in it, giving that stillness a stated human purpose. | terra: Allah makes the night لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ and the day visible, stating the night's divinely given stillness.

luna: The section’s dictionary form استودعته means leaving something with another for safekeeping; “مُسْتَوْدَعَهَا” is paired with every creature’s settled place, and God knows both, making entrusted keeping part of divine provision. | terra: مُسْتَقَرَّهَا وَمُسْتَوْدَعَهَا directly joins each creature's settled place and deposited place under Allah's knowledge, while its provision remains His charge.
terra: Noah says وَمَا أَنَا بِطَارِدِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا, refusing the elite's demand that he expel the believers who have joined him.
terra: Noah asks who could help him against Allah if he drove the believers away, making abandonment of the vulnerable a breach of divine protection.
terra: Noah builds the ark بِأَعْيُنِنَا وَوَحْيِنَا, making the vessel that will keep its passengers a work under divine sight.
terra: Noah calls his separated son to board with the family and not remain with the unbelievers, supplying the offered refuge that the son refuses in 11:43.
terra: Noah's son says سَآوِي إِلَىٰ جَبَلٍ, but the mountain cannot protect him and the wave separates them; the ayah distinguishes false refuge from the mercy that truly shelters.
terra: Noah is told to disembark with peace and blessings, completing the ark's temporary custody in a divinely secured new settlement.

luna: The section names dwelling as a secondary sense of the root غ ن ي; this verse says Thamud became as if they had never lived in their homes, a specific reversal of remaining settled. | terra: كَأَن لَّمْ يَغْنَوْا فِيهَا says Thamud's settled presence vanished as though they had never dwelt there, exposing how a dwelling can fail to remain.
terra: Lot wishes for power or a strong support to which he might take refuge, using the section's sheltering verb to name the protection his exposed household needs.
terra: The angels assure Lot that his enemies will not reach him and command a protected night departure with his family, while specifying the boundary represented by his wife.

luna: The section’s dictionary form غني القوم في دارهم means dwelling in one’s home; this verse says Midian became as if they had never lived there, making departure and erasure the opposite of staying. | terra: Madyan too becomes كَأَن لَّمْ يَغْنَوْا فِيهَا, another direct Qur'anic occurrence of the section's secondary غ ن ي sense of long residence.

luna: The section distinguishes departure from being actively driven away; Joseph’s brother proposes casting him into the well so a traveler will pick him up, a plan to remove him that leaves his safety precarious. | terra: A brother proposes putting Joseph in the hidden depth of a well so a caravan will pick him up, a calculated scene of leaving a child behind.
terra: Jacob fears that the brothers will take Joseph away and that a wolf will eat him while they are heedless, directly joining departure to the danger of neglected care.

luna: The section says a person can be left behind yet not abandoned by God; after Joseph’s brothers cast him into the well, God reveals that he will later remind them of what they did. | terra: When Joseph is actually placed in the well, revelation reaches him there and promises a future reckoning, showing divine address continuing inside human abandonment.
terra: The brothers' lie says they left Joseph beside their belongings while they raced; even as fabricated speech, it precisely pictures a person left behind and exposed.

luna: The section joins being left with being taken in; after Joseph is cast into a well in 12:15, a passing caravan finds him and treats him as a valuable discovery, reversing his brothers’ abandonment. | terra: A caravan draws Joseph from the well and hides him as merchandise; it ends literal abandonment while exposing him to another kind of concealment and loss of kin.

luna: The section’s فآوى means bringing someone close and sheltering him; after Joseph is sold away from his family, the Egyptian who buys him tells his wife to give him an honorable lodging and considers adopting him. | terra: After the well and sale, Joseph is given an honored lodging and possible adoption in Egypt; shelter answers the brothers' act of disposal.
terra: A released prisoner forgets Joseph, so فَلَبِثَ فِي السِّجْنِ بِضْعَ سِنِينَ; human forgetting leaves him to remain confined, unlike the Lord who does not forget.
terra: The former prisoner remembers Joseph after a long interval, ending the human forgetting that had left him confined in 12:42.
terra: Joseph tells the people to leave harvested grain فِي سُنبُلِهِ, in its own enclosing ear, so “leaving” the provision is precisely how it is preserved.
terra: The hard years consume the stored harvest except a little مِمَّا تُحْصِنُونَ; it states the protective result of the leaving-in-the-ear act in 12:47.

luna: The section’s image moves from being left to being taken in; after Joseph’s confinement and release, this verse has the king receive him and call him established and trusted, a reversal of his earlier abandonment.

luna: The section’s dictionary form استودعته means entrusting something for safekeeping; this neighboring verse has Joseph ask to oversee the land’s storehouses as a knowledgeable guardian. | terra: Joseph asks to be placed over the land's storehouses because he is a knowing guardian, making preservation of hidden provision an explicit office.

luna: The section’s root gloss for غ ن ي includes people dwelling in their home; this neighboring verse says God established Joseph in the land, where he could settle as he wished, after his earlier abandonment. | terra: After the well, sale, and prison, Allah establishes Joseph in the land so he may settle wherever he wishes, answering successive displacements with secure residence.

luna: The section’s dictionary form استودعته means entrusting something to another for protection; Jacob asks whether he should entrust Benjamin to his brothers again and says God is the best keeper, recalling their earlier betrayal of Joseph. | terra: As Jacob must release another son to his brothers, فَاللَّهُ خَيْرٌ حَافِظًا makes Allah the better keeper of the one being entrusted away from home.
terra: Jacob sends the son only after a binding pledge and ends اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ مَا نَقُولُ وَكِيلٌ, placing the risky departure under divine trusteeship.
terra: آوَىٰ إِلَيْهِ أَخَاهُ uses the section's sheltering verb for Joseph drawing his brother to himself after the family's long separation.
terra: آوَىٰ إِلَيْهِ أَبَوَيْهِ uses the same verb for Joseph receiving his parents, so the root marks reunion and taking-in rather than departure.
terra: Floodwater carries passing foam while مَا يَنفَعُ النَّاسَ فَيَمْكُثُ فِي الْأَرْضِ; the ayah makes vanishing and remaining visible in one scene.
terra: Those who join what Allah commanded to be joined supply the positive relation opposite the source explanation's “he did not cut the bond.”
terra: Breaking Allah's covenant and cutting what He commanded joined repeats the relational rupture excluded from the Lord-Prophet bond.
terra: Allah effaces or confirms what He wills while the Mother of the Book remains with Him, directly juxtaposing removal and establishment under divine possession.

luna: The section distinguishes a servant’s rejection from the Lord’s care; here disbelievers tell their messengers they will expel them unless they return, while God promises to destroy the wrongdoers. | terra: The disbelievers threaten their messengers with expulsion from the land; the Lord answers the threatened departure with a promise to destroy the wrongdoers.
terra: وَلَنُسْكِنَنَّكُمُ الْأَرْضَ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ completes 14:13 by replacing threatened expulsion with settlement granted by the Lord.
terra: A good word is a good tree with a firm root, a living picture of what is made stable and continues to give.
terra: The bad word is uprooted and has مِن قَرَارٍ no stability, the exact opposite of a protected or abiding placement.
terra: Abraham says he has settled part of his offspring in an uncultivated valley and asks their Lord to draw hearts and provide fruit, a family left in divine care rather than discarded.
terra: Allah says He sent the Reminder and will guard it, a textual instance of something given forth yet continuously preserved.
terra: Lot is told to travel with his family during part of the night, follow behind them, and let none turn back, making departure itself the divinely guarded route of rescue.
luna: The section’s denial of abandonment addresses prophetic distress; here God says He knows the Prophet’s breast is constricted by what people say, naming the hurt behind such reassurance.
luna: The section’s reassurance is followed by worship rather than isolation; this neighboring verse tells the Prophet to glorify his Lord and prostrate in response to the distress named in 15:97.
luna: The section puts continuing divine care beside the Prophet’s distress; this neighboring verse commands worship of the Lord until certainty comes, extending the response in 15:98.

luna: The section links separation with refuge and provision; this verse says those who emigrated after being wronged will be settled well in this world, a direct answer to forced departure. | terra: Those who migrate after wrong will be given a good worldly lodging by Allah, so departure under pressure leads to divinely granted settlement.
terra: Permanent houses and light tents for travel show dwelling and departure as complementary provisions rather than abandonment.

luna: The section describes a garment being preserved in a case; this verse reverses the direction of protection by describing garments that shield people from heat and armor that protects them from one another. | terra: Garments protect people from heat and violence, reversing the source dictionary example's direction: there the garment itself is put into a cover that protects it.
terra: مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ اللَّهِ بَاقٍ states the image's distinction exactly: what is held by people runs out, while what is with Allah remains.

luna: The section’s reassurance is about care after abandonment; this verse speaks of people who emigrated after persecution, struggled, and remained patient, then names their Lord as forgiving and merciful.
terra: A town once secure and amply provided is made to taste hunger and fear after ingratitude, reversing the shelter-and-provision pattern.
luna: The section notes that ر ب ب can name staying; this verse uses the related root in “رَبَّيَانِي” for parents raising a child, connecting the word family to sustained care for the young.

luna: The section’s sheltering of an orphan reverses neglect; this command forbids approaching an orphan’s property except in the best way until maturity. | terra: The same boundary around orphan property lasts until maturity and is joined to fulfillment of the covenant, making guardianship accountable.
terra: The Prophet's opponents nearly drive him from the land, yet the ayah says they themselves would remain after him only briefly.
terra: After the expulsion warning in 17:76, the unchanged divine way with earlier messengers says such removal cannot displace the Lord's enduring pattern.
terra: The arrival of truth makes falsehood vanish because falsehood is inherently vanishing, a clear boundary between what remains and what cannot.

luna: The section names the cave youths’ refuge in 18:16; here they ask their Lord for mercy and right guidance as they withdraw to the cave, giving the refuge its own prayerful beginning. | terra: The youths أَوَى الْفِتْيَةُ إِلَى الْكَهْفِ and ask their Lord for mercy and right guidance, the voluntary act of joining a refuge.
terra: Allah seals the youths' hearing in the cave for counted years, making the refuge a place of sustained protected stillness.

luna: The section’s youths find refuge after leaving their people in 18:16; this scene says God strengthened their hearts as they stood against their people, supplying the resolve that precedes refuge.

luna: The section glosses فآوى as joining someone and giving refuge; these youths leave their people and are told “فَأْوُوا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ,” trusting their Lord to spread mercy over them. | terra: The youths' withdrawal from their people becomes refuge rather than abandonment: they are told to take shelter in the cave so their Lord will spread mercy and prepare ease.
terra: The sun's course avoids the sleepers while they lie in an opening of the cave, detailing how their chosen refuge becomes a protected environment.
terra: The sleepers are turned right and left while their dog guards the entrance, showing their hidden bodies actively preserved during the long stay.
terra: The youths explain that discovery would mean stoning or forced return to unbelief, specifying the danger from which the cave keeps them.
terra: The stated centuries of the youths' stay make the cave's protective duration explicit rather than merely implied.
terra: After the cave's long preservation, the ayah says Allah best knows how long the youths remained and that they have no protector besides Him, joining duration to exclusive guardianship.
terra: The Prophet is told to keep himself patiently with those who call their Lord and not let his eyes pass beyond them, the positive act opposed to driving them away.
terra: Worldly life is rain-grown vegetation that becomes dry debris scattered by winds, a concrete image of what does not stay.
terra: Beside 18:45's scattered growth, الْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ are better with the Lord, supplying what remains.

luna: The section explains the orphan as one liable to be neglected; here two orphans’ treasure is guarded until they mature, by their Lord’s mercy, so their father’s goodness can continue protecting them after his death. | terra: A wall conceals treasure belonging to two orphans until maturity, making the Lord's unseen protection of an orphaned deposit the opposite of neglected care.
terra: Zakaria fears what will happen after he is gone while his wife is barren, so his request for an heir grows directly from anxiety about what departure leaves exposed.
terra: He asks for an heir who will inherit from him and Jacob's house and be pleasing to the Lord, specifying the continuing relation sought in 19:5.

luna: The section’s dictionary form قلا describes driving away; Abraham’s father threatens him and says “leave me for a long while,” a concrete human rejection set against the Lord’s refusal to abandon His servant. | terra: Abraham's father threatens stoning and orders وَاهْجُرْنِي مَلِيًّا, making familial expulsion the human rupture that the following ayat answer.

luna: The section distinguishes departure from divine abandonment; Abraham says he will leave his father and his people’s worship, showing a chosen separation from people and false gods rather than a rejected servant. | terra: Abraham withdraws from his people and their objects of worship while continuing to call on his Lord, so human separation does not become separation from God.

luna: The section places care after separation; this neighboring verse says that after Abraham leaves his people, God grants him Isaac and Jacob, so departure is followed by new family and prophetic care. | terra: When Abraham withdraws, Allah grants him Isaac and Jacob and makes them prophets, replacing lost family company with a divinely given family.

luna: The section’s root gloss links the Lord’s name with remaining; here the descending messengers say they come only by His command and conclude that He is not forgetful, directly answering the fear of being left. | terra: The descending messengers explain an apparent interval by saying they descend only at the Lord's command and وَمَا كَانَ رَبُّكَ نَسِيًّا, directly excluding forgetful abandonment by “your Lord.”
terra: The enduring good deeds are again said to be better with the Lord in reward and return, a repeated direct formulation of what remains.
terra: Allah inherits what the boastful person claims and that person comes to Him alone, another separation of the departing human from retained possessions.
terra: The guilty are driven thirsty to Hell, another direct occurrence of the source dictionary's leading-away action with an openly punitive destination.

luna: The section’s image joins separation with continued care; Moses is placed in a chest and cast into the river, yet God says He cast love over him and raised him under His eye. | terra: The infant is placed in a chest and cast into the river, yet the command ends with his being formed عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي, a literal deposit kept under divine sight.

terra: This single retrospective ayah returns Moses to his mother, rescues him after the killing, keeps him for years among Midian's people, and brings him back according to measure, repeatedly turning exposure and departure into care.

luna: The section’s denial of divine severance meets God’s direct reassurance to Moses and Aaron, “إِنَّنِي مَعَكُمَا”: He is with them, hearing and seeing, when they fear Pharaoh. | terra: To two frightened messengers Allah says إِنَّنِي مَعَكُمَا أَسْمَعُ وَأَرَى, turning feared exposure before Pharaoh into heard, seen companionship.

luna: The section cites the claim that the Lord is not forgetful; Moses answers Pharaoh that his Lord neither errs nor forgets (“وَلَا يَنسَىٰ”), repeating the image’s assurance in a different prophetic scene. | terra: Moses says his Lord's knowledge is in a record and لَا يَضِلُّ رَبِّي وَلَا يَنسَىٰ, another explicit denial of divine forgetting.
terra: The magicians tell Pharaoh that Allah is better and more enduring, choosing the abiding Lord over a ruler's immediate threat.
terra: Moses is commanded to leave by night with Allah's servants and make a dry sea path without fear of being overtaken, a departure whose way is prepared and guarded.

luna: The section cites “your Lord is not forgetful”; here the wrongdoer first neglected God’s signs and is told, “today you are forgotten,” making human neglect the explicit reversal. | terra: The one who forgot Allah's signs is told وَكَذَٰلِكَ الْيَوْمَ تُنسَىٰ, a deliberate being-left-out in judgment that sharpens the positive assurance to the Prophet.
terra: The Prophet is told not to strain his eyes toward temporary worldly splendor because his Lord's provision is better and more enduring.
terra: Truth is hurled against falsehood until it crushes it and falsehood vanishes, another active formulation of what cannot remain.
terra: David is taught to make armor that protects people from violence, another crafted covering whose function is safekeeping.
terra: Jonah goes away in anger, then calls from layered darkness and confesses; the scene tests the thought that departure could put him beyond his Lord's power or hearing.
terra: Allah answers Jonah, rescues him from distress, and generalizes that rescue to believers, explicitly resolving the departure-and-darkness scene.
terra: Zakaria's plea رَبِّ لَا تَذَرْنِي فَرْدًا directly asks his Lord not to leave him solitary.
terra: Allah answers 21:89 by granting Yahya and making his wife fit, replacing feared solitary abandonment with a household and divine response.
terra: Allah declares that He defends those who believe, supplying a general protection claim immediately before the expulsion scene of 22:40.
terra: People expelled from homes unjustly are placed under Allah's defense, and the ayah promises that He surely supports those who support Him.

luna: The section joins departure with enrichment; this verse says those who emigrate for God and then die or are killed will receive good provision from Him, so departure does not end divine provision.

luna: The section develops leaving a deposit with another for preservation; this verse describes believers as guarding their trusts and covenants, a human counterpart to faithful safekeeping. | terra: Believers who faithfully observe their trusts enact the keeper's side of the section's deposited-object relation.
terra: A human beginning is placed as a drop فِي قَرَارٍ مَّكِينٍ, a secure receptacle that holds what has been deposited for development.
terra: Noah is told to place paired creatures and his family in the ark when the flood begins, so threatened lives are gathered into a protective vessel.
terra: Noah's prayer asks his Lord to bring him to a blessed landing and names Him the best giver of lodging, explicitly entrusting the end of the voyage to divine settlement.
terra: وَآوَيْنَاهُمَا إِلَىٰ رَبْوَةٍ ذَاتِ قَرَارٍ وَمَعِينٍ joins divine sheltering of Mary and Jesus to a secure place of settlement and provision.

luna: The section’s عائلًا فأغنى presents need answered by provision; this verse says that if those marrying are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty (“يُغْنِهِمُ اللَّهُ”). | terra: Poor prospective spouses are promised that Allah will enrich them from His bounty, repeating the transition from need to sufficiency.
terra: Those unable to marry are told to remain chaste until Allah enriches them, placing patient need under anticipated divine sufficiency.
terra: Allah drives clouds, joins them, and makes them a mass before rain descends; the source dictionary's lingering cloud is here mobile and gathered under command.

luna: The section says the Lord did not leave the Prophet; here the Prophet laments that his people have abandoned the Quran (“مَهْجُورًا”), reversing who has severed the relation. | terra: The Messenger complains يَا رَبِّ that his people took this Qur'an مَهْجُورًا; human abandonment of the message stands against the Lord's non-abandonment of the Messenger.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss says the root ر ب ب can describe a cloud that lasts; this verse pictures the Lord extending shade and says He could have made it stationary, placing continuance under divine control.

luna: The section pairs staying with departure; this neighboring verse says God withdraws the extended shade little by little, making a measured withdrawal the counterpart to the stationary shade of 25:45.

luna: The section presents the night as settled before the denial of separation; this verse calls night a covering and sleep a rest, joining darkness to repose. | terra: Allah makes night a covering, sleep repose, and day a rising, expanding the settled-night image into enclosure, rest, and renewed departure.
terra: وَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى الْحَيِّ الَّذِي لَا يَمُوتُ tells the Prophet to entrust himself to the One whose life never departs.
terra: Before Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh, Allah rejects their fear and says that He is with them, listening; it is a second direct assurance that the messengers will not be left alone.

luna: The section links the Lord’s name with staying and develops the taking-in of a vulnerable child; Pharaoh says “أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا” (“did we not raise you among us”), showing the same root family used for raising rather than staying. | terra: Pharaoh recalls that Moses was raised in his household as a child and remained there for years, a true sheltering history voiced as a hostile claim of ownership.
terra: With the sea ahead and Pharaoh behind, Moses answers his companions' fear with كَلَّا إِنَّ مَعِيَ رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ, confidence that his Lord has not left him.
terra: وَمَا أَنَا بِطَارِدِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ repeats a messenger's refusal to drive believers away, directly reversing the source dictionary's driving scene.
terra: Lot says إِنِّي لِعَمَلِكُم مِّنَ الْقَالِينَ: the section's ق ل ي root is actual detestation here, directed at a people's deed, whereas 93:3 denies that the Lord treats the Prophet so.
terra: The only answer of Lot's people is again to order his family expelled, because they are people who keep themselves pure.
terra: Allah then saves Lot and his family except the wife whose remaining with the condemned is decreed.
terra: The ayah again says Allah made night so people may rest in it and day to give sight, the same night-as-repose relation.

luna: The section joins separation with continued care; God tells Moses’ mother to place him in the river but promises, “إِنَّا رَادُّوهُ إِلَيْكِ,” that He will return him to her. | terra: Moses' mother is told to cast her infant into the river without fear or grief because Allah promises to return him; relinquishing the child becomes divine safekeeping.
terra: Pharaoh's household picks the cast-away infant from the river; this is the first human reception of the child entrusted to the water, though the ayah also foretells later enmity and grief.

luna: The section’s orphan image is of a vulnerable child received into care; Pharaoh’s wife asks that the infant Moses be spared and kept, opening the household refuge that follows his separation from his mother. | terra: Pharaoh's wife calls Moses a comfort to the eye, forbids killing him, and proposes taking him as a son, converting the abandoned infant's arrival into household shelter.
terra: After Moses refuses other nurses, his sister directs the household to a family who will care for him sincerely, the concrete means by which the deposited child is preserved and returned.

luna: The section places shelter after separation; this later part of Moses’ story returns him to his mother so her eye may be comforted and she may not grieve, completing the rescue begun in 28:9. | terra: فَرَدَدْنَاهُ إِلَىٰ أُمِّهِ completes the river scene: the child entrusted beyond his mother's reach is returned so her eye may be comforted and she may know the promise true.
terra: Moses leaves the city fearful and watchful while asking his Lord for rescue, initiating a vulnerable departure that reaches safety in 28:25.
terra: As Moses turns toward Midian he hopes his Lord will guide him to the right way, entrusting the route after flight to divine direction.
luna: The section’s عائلًا فأغنى depicts need met by provision; after Moses helps two women and rests in shade, he asks his Lord for whatever good He sends, naming his own dependence.
terra: At the Midian household Moses is told not to fear because he has escaped the wrongdoing people, marking arrival at human shelter after flight.
terra: Destroyed settlements become dwellings scarcely inhabited after their people, and Allah remains the inheritor; residence, departure, and what remains are held together.
terra: The counterfactual of night made perpetual asks who could bring light, placing permanence itself under the Lord's control.
terra: The counterfactual of day made perpetual asks who could bring a night in which people rest, clarifying that settled night is a continuing gift rather than neglect.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss for سجا includes quiet and duration; this verse says God made night for rest and day for seeking bounty, framing rest as part of mercy. | terra: From His mercy Allah gives both night for rest and day for seeking bounty, making stillness and provision alternating forms of care.
terra: كُلُّ شَيْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ gives the same ultimate boundary between what departs and the One who does not.

luna: The section develops departure alongside the Lord’s continued care; Abraham says he is emigrating to his Lord (“إِنِّي مُهَاجِرٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي”), making departure an approach toward divine protection rather than rejection.
terra: Allah leaves from Lot's destroyed town a clear sign for people who understand, making a remnant preserve the lesson of those who departed.
terra: The present life is called play and diversion while the hereafter is the real life, distinguishing temporary appearance from enduring reality.
luna: The section glosses the night in 93:2 as settled and lasting; this verse names sleep at night and day among God’s signs, connecting the night’s rest to daily human life.
terra: Winds raise and spread clouds, then rain emerges; against the source dictionary's cloud that stays, this cloud's movement is the means of provision.

luna: The section’s reassurance that God does not forget is bounded by this judgment: those who forgot the meeting of this day are told to taste the consequence of having forgotten it. | terra: إِنَّا نَسِينَاكُمْ answers people's forgetting of the meeting with punitive abandonment, a specific reversal of divine remembrance and care.

luna: The section names the dictionary form ودّع as leaving or cutting a tie; here the command is “وَدَعْ أَذَاهُمْ,” to leave their harm, distinguishing withdrawal from an abuser’s conduct from abandoning the person addressed. | terra: The command وَدَعْ أَذَاهُمْ uses the section's و د ع root but makes their harm, rather than the Prophet, what is left; the same ayah tells him to entrust himself to Allah as Trustee.
terra: Allah sends winds that raise a cloud and drives it to dead land, another mobile-cloud reversal whose destination restores life.
terra: The descendants carried in the laden ship are made a sign, another compact picture of lives held and transported through danger.
terra: After Noah's rescue, Allah makes his descendants the survivors, so the flood narrative identifies who is made to remain.
terra: Allah leaves Noah's honored remembrance among later generations, an explicit instance of leaving as preservation through time.
luna: The section distinguishes being left by God from leaving people; Abraham says he is going to his Lord (“إِنِّي ذَاهِبٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي”) and trusts that He will guide him.
terra: The same formula leaves Abraham's remembrance among later generations, repeating the positive sense of a legacy made to remain.
terra: Moses and Aaron likewise have their remembrance left among later generations after rescue and support.
terra: Elijah's remembrance is left among later generations, completing another repeated formulation of enduring honor.
terra: Jonah's own glorification is named as the condition that precedes his release from the fish, showing relation with Allah persisting inside confinement.
terra: The counterfactual says Jonah would have remained in the fish until resurrection, turning “remaining” into the fate from which divine response releases him.
terra: Allah casts the sick Jonah onto the open shore, a scene of apparent disposal whose protective continuation comes in 37:146.
terra: Allah grows a broad-leaved plant over Jonah, placing cover and care directly over the exposed body on the shore.
terra: Human beings are formed in their mothers' wombs through darkness layered upon darkness, a hidden enclosure in which creation is kept through stages.
terra: أَلَيْسَ اللَّهُ بِكَافٍ عَبْدَهُ reassures the threatened servant that Allah is sufficient for him while others try to frighten him.
terra: The unbelievers are driven to Hell in groups, directly realizing the “drive and lead” action in the source explanation of قَلَىٰ as punitive expulsion.
terra: The God-fearing are also led in groups, but to the Garden, showing that being driven onward can end in reception rather than rejection.
terra: إِنَّمَا هَذِهِ الْحَيَاةُ الدُّنْيَا مَتَاعٌ وَإِنَّ الْآخِرَةَ هِيَ دَارُ الْقَرَارِ names the near life as passing use and the hereafter as the abiding home.

luna: The section foregrounds the night’s stillness; this verse says God made night so people may rest in it, then calls daylight a means of seeing. | terra: Allah makes night لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ and day seeing, another direct formulation of the settled-night image.
terra: If Allah stills the wind, ships remain رَوَاكِدَ on the sea, a non-night scene that nevertheless joins cessation to continued stillness.
terra: Worldly gifts are temporary enjoyment, while what is with Allah is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, another explicit passing-versus-abiding statement.
luna: The section joins night with the message that messengers descend by their Lord’s command; this verse says revelation was sent down on a blessed night.
luna: The section’s image moves from settled night to divine assurance; this neighboring verse says every wise matter is apportioned on that night, giving the revelation a measured purpose.
luna: The section cites descent by the Lord’s command; this neighboring verse identifies the night’s apportionment as a command from God, clarifying who governs what comes down.

luna: The section presents the Lord as one who does not abandon and shelters the vulnerable; this neighboring verse calls the command mercy from the Lord, giving the night’s revelation a stated care-giving purpose.
terra: Pharaoh's people leave behind gardens and springs, showing possessions and dwellings remaining after their owners are forced away.
terra: What Pharaoh's people leave is inherited by another people, clarifying that departure changes custody rather than making the goods disappear.

luna: The section says the Lord is not forgetful; this judgment says, “today We forget you as you forgot the meeting of this day,” a direct reversal grounded in their own neglect. | terra: الْيَوْمَ نَنسَاكُمْ repeats the judgment formula for those who forgot their meeting, showing where “not forgotten” no longer applies as relational favor.

luna: The section’s denial of abandonment meets the consequence stated here: they are left in the Fire because they took God’s signs in mockery and worldly life deceived them, completing 45:34’s judgment.
terra: Believers who support Allah's cause are promised His support and the firming of their feet, a reciprocal form of not being left unsupported.
terra: The Prophet is addressed through the fate of towns stronger than the town that expelled him, placing his forced departure under a divine reversal.
terra: وَتُقَطِّعُوا أَرْحَامَكُمْ makes severing kinship a condemned human act, clarifying the social force of a bond being cut.
terra: وَاللَّهُ مَعَكُمْ وَلَن يَتِرَكُمْ أَعْمَالَكُمْ joins divine companionship to a promise that believers' deeds will not be deprived of their due.
luna: The section says the needy person was met with enrichment; this verse assigns the asker and deprived a right in the wealthy people’s property, turning provision into an obligation.
terra: A sign is left in the same punished settlement for those who fear painful punishment, another purposeful remnant after destruction.
terra: The Prophet is told to endure his Lord's judgment because فَإِنَّكَ بِأَعْيُنِنَا, an explicit assurance of watchful keeping.

luna: The section’s root gloss for فأغنى includes being made rich; this verse says God is the one who “أَغْنَىٰ,” directly naming the provision that answers need. | terra: وَأَنَّهُ هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ attributes enrichment and lasting provision to Allah, directly paralleling فَأَغْنَىٰ.
terra: The ark sails بِأَعْيُنِنَا as recompense for the rejected Noah, another scene of a threatened servant and his charge preserved under divine watching.
terra: The flood vessel or its story is left as a sign for remembrance, making what is left behind something intentionally preserved rather than discarded.
terra: كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍ names everything that passes away, supplying the departing half of the section's leaving-and-remaining relation completed in 55:27.
terra: وَيَبْقَىٰ وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ places “your Lord” with what remains after all else perishes, giving Qur'anic force to the source dictionary's abiding sense beside رَبّ.
terra: The noble Qur'an is identified as the precious object whose enclosing place is named in 56:78.
terra: The Qur'an is located in a protected or hidden book, paralleling the source dictionary's valuable object enclosed for preservation.
terra: Allah is said to be with people wherever they are and to see what they do, a universal statement of presence behind the section's personal reassurance.
terra: Worldly life is vegetation that pleases, yellows, and becomes debris; its staged decay makes the instability of present possession visible.
luna: The section shows need answered by giving; this verse includes orphans among the recipients of redistributed property and says wealth should not circulate only among the rich.

luna: The section distinguishes being left behind from being cared for; this verse describes poor emigrants expelled from homes and property, who seek God’s bounty and support His cause. | terra: The emigrants are expelled from homes and property, supplying the forced departure to which the settled hosts of 59:9 respond.

luna: The section’s image of need met with shelter is enacted by the hosts who welcome emigrants and prefer them over themselves (“وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ”), even when they themselves are in need. | terra: Those who settled in the Home love the emigrants who come to them and prefer them despite need, turning one group's displacement into another group's reception.
terra: Those who forget Allah are made to forget themselves, a moral consequence that clarifies the destructive form of forgetfulness against divine remembering care.
terra: The enemies' expulsion of the Messenger and believers is named while believers are warned not to entrust affection to them.
terra: Whoever entrusts himself to Allah finds Him sufficient; the same ayah says every matter has a divinely set measure.

luna: The section’s عائلًا فأغنى joins need to provision; this verse instructs a person of means and a person with restricted provision to spend according to what God has given each, making support responsive to need.
terra: In a moment of household opposition, the ayah declares Allah the Prophet's protector, followed by Gabriel, righteous believers, and angels as supporters.

terra: The Prophet is told to wait patiently for his Lord's judgment and not be like Jonah when he called out in distress, introducing a messenger who left and nevertheless remained within divine response.
terra: The ayah says that without favor overtaking Jonah he would have been cast blameworthy onto the bare shore, making divine grace the intervention against discarded exposure.
terra: Jonah's Lord then chooses him and makes him one of the righteous, completing the movement from flight and casting-out to restored election.
terra: When the water overflowed, Allah carried human forebears in the vessel, presenting the ark as collective safekeeping.
terra: The condemned speaker says his wealth did not avail him, another boundary showing that worldly sufficiency cannot keep its owner.
luna: The section’s image ends in provision for need; this verse describes the condemned person as one who did not encourage feeding the poor, a specific opposite of enrichment.
luna: The section’s need-to-enrichment image meets this statement that some wealth has a known right; 70:25 specifies the recipients as the asker and deprived.
luna: The section’s provision for the needy is made concrete here: the known right in 70:24 belongs to the asker and the deprived.

luna: The section’s dictionary form وديعة means a deposit entrusted to another; this verse repeats the quality of guarding trusts and covenants, making the duty of keeping them explicit. | terra: The same description of guarding trusts and covenants repeats safekeeping as a defining faithful practice.

luna: The section’s image distinguishes rejection from care; here the Prophet is told to bear their words and avoid them graciously, a boundary showing that withdrawal from harm need not mean being forsaken. | terra: وَاهْجُرْهُمْ هَجْرًا جَمِيلًا commands the Prophet to withdraw graciously from hostile speakers, using the very هجر wording by which the source dictionary explains severed farewell.

luna: The section glosses سجا as a night that remains; this oath instead marks night as it withdraws, a direct reversal that makes the distinction between settling and departing visible. | terra: وَاللَّيْلِ إِذْ أَدْبَرَ swears by night as it retreats, a direct moving-away counterpart to the night when it settles in 93:2.
luna: The section’s image ends with need met by provision; in the account of those in the Fire, this verse names their failure to feed the poor as one reason for their condemnation.

luna: The section’s dictionary form قلا العير آتنه describes a wild ass driving its mares away; this verse compares people fleeing to “حُمُرٌ مُّسْتَنفِرَةٌ,” reversing the agency, and 74:51 names the lion they flee from. | terra: The people are likened to startled donkeys; this recalls the source dictionary's wild-ass scene, though here the animals are the fleeing group rather than a male driving females.

luna: The section’s wild-ass dictionary scene has the male driving the mares; this neighboring verse identifies the wild asses’ pursuer as a lion, completing the reversal in 74:50. | terra: فَرَّتْ مِن قَسْوَرَةٍ completes 74:50 with flight from a pursuer; the link to the source's driven herd is concrete but the agent and direction differ.
terra: أَيَحْسَبُ الْإِنسَانُ أَن يُتْرَكَ سُدًى rejects the idea that a human is left unattended or without purpose, a general boundary around abandonment.

luna: The section’s provision answers vulnerability; this verse depicts the righteous feeding an orphan, the poor, and a captive despite their own love of the food. | terra: Feeding an orphan despite love of the food supplies a concrete act of care for the one the section says is commonly overlooked.
terra: فَجَعَلْنَاهُ فِي قَرَارٍ مَّكِينٍ repeats the image of vulnerable life placed and kept in a secure lodging.
terra: The secure womb-deposit of 77:21 is retained until a known measure, adding bounded duration to protected placement.
luna: The section glosses سجا as becoming still (“سكن”); this verse calls sleep “سُبَاتًا,” a cessation and rest that gives another Quranic formulation of stillness.
luna: The section’s night settles before the statement that God has not departed; this verse calls night a covering (“لِبَاسًا”), giving the dark its enveloping quality.
luna: The section sets the still night before the reassurance; this neighboring verse makes the day a time of livelihood, completing the night-rest/day-activity contrast following 78:10.

luna: The section joins unmet need with taking the vulnerable in; here the Prophet frowns and turns away at a visitor, a concrete reversed response to the surah’s instruction not to rebuff the asker. | terra: عَبَسَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ supplies the turning-away act; 80:2 identifies the vulnerable blind man from whom the turn occurs.

luna: The section’s image includes a person in need; this neighboring verse identifies the visitor as a blind man who comes, explaining the vulnerable person at whom the Prophet turned away in 80:1. | terra: The blind man comes to the Prophet, completing the encounter in which 80:1 stages relational withdrawal rather than reception.
luna: The section’s orphan-care image treats vulnerability as a reason for attention; this neighboring verse says the blind visitor might be purified, explaining the possible good in receiving him.
luna: The section’s image makes care for the vulnerable perceptible; this neighboring verse says the visitor may take a reminder and benefit from it, continuing the reason to attend to him.

luna: The section’s needy person is the one who receives provision; this verse introduces the person who considers himself self-sufficient, the contrasting figure who receives the Prophet’s attention in 80:6. | terra: أَمَّا مَنِ اسْتَغْنَىٰ uses غ ن ي for one who deems himself self-sufficient; attention goes toward him while the seeking man is neglected.
luna: The section’s need-to-care image is reversed here: this neighboring verse says the Prophet gives his attention to the self-sufficient person introduced in 80:5.
luna: The section makes care independent of whether the recipient can repay it; this neighboring verse says the Prophet is not accountable if the self-sufficient man does not purify himself.
luna: The section says a person in need should not be left; this neighboring verse turns back to someone who comes striving to the Prophet, contrasting the seeker with the self-sufficient man.
luna: The section’s image gives attention to vulnerability; this neighboring verse adds that the seeker fears God, specifying what makes his approach spiritually urgent.

luna: The section’s sheltering and provision reverse neglect; this neighboring verse concludes that the Prophet turns away from the fearful seeker, directly echoing the surah’s prohibition on rebuffing its asker. | terra: فَأَنتَ عَنْهُ تَلَهَّىٰ identifies inattention to the one who came striving and fearing in 80:8-9, a direct instance of overlooked care.
terra: وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا عَسْعَسَ presents night at a transition of approach or retreat, illuminating by contrast the unambiguous stillness stressed in the section.
terra: بَلْ هُوَ قُرْآنٌ مَّجِيدٌ names the precious thing whose protected enclosure is specified in 85:22.
terra: فِي لَوْحٍ مَّحْفُوظٍ places the Qur'an in a guarded tablet, paralleling the source dictionary's object kept inside a protective case.
terra: بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا identifies the human preference for what is nearer and passing.
terra: وَالْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ supplies the enduring counterpart to 87:16 and closely matches the surah's wider better-later horizon.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss gives the night duration and stillness; this oath marks night as it passes on, the opposite temporal movement. | terra: وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَسْرِ depicts night journeying on, reversing the source section's night that becomes still and lasts.

luna: The section reads sheltering the orphan as the opposite of neglect; this rebuke says people fail even to honor the orphan (“لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ”). | terra: بَل لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ names failure to honor the orphan, the neglect from which the section derives the name يَتِيم.
luna: The section’s فأغنى answers need; this rebuke condemns failure to encourage feeding the poor, giving that provision a neglected social counterpart.

luna: The section shows need answered with provision; this neighboring verse names feeding people on a day of famine as part of the difficult path, setting up the orphan in 90:15 and the poor in 90:16.

luna: The section’s orphan is a vulnerable person who needs care; this verse identifies feeding an orphan who is a relative as one of the hard paths of goodness. | terra: Feeding an orphan of near kin on a day of hunger joins family attachment to material care rather than neglect.
luna: The section’s needy person is met with provision; this neighboring verse names feeding a poor person in misery, completing the vulnerable recipients listed around 90:15.
luna: The section’s night is glossed as settled and lasting; this oath depicts night as it covers the day, a distinct but related movement into darkness.
luna: The section emphasizes night as still and lasting; this oath depicts night as it covers, a related night image that emphasizes concealment rather than settling.
terra: The one who deems himself self-sufficient uses the غ ن ي family for a false independence, reversing the sufficiency Allah grants to the needy.
terra: A person's wealth will not avail him when he falls, opposing stored wealth to the care that truly suffices.
terra: The human transgresses because he sees himself self-sufficient, showing the corrupt counterfeit of the enrichment given by the Lord.

luna: The section brings a settled night before its reassurance and cites descent by the Lord’s command; this verse says the Quran was sent down during the Night of Decree, meeting night and revelation in one scene.

luna: The section quotes messengers saying their descent occurs only by their Lord’s command; this verse says angels and the Spirit descend by their Lord’s permission for every matter during that night.
luna: The section glosses the night as enduring stillness; this neighboring verse calls the night peace until dawn, specifying a span of calm.
terra: The panting chargers recall the source dictionary's horse released into open country, though the ayah depicts running and does not itself say the horses were abandoned or let loose.
terra: The Lord who feeds against hunger and grants safety against fear supplies the compact positive answer to need and exposure.

luna: The section says the orphan’s name is linked in its dictionary explanation to neglected kindness, and contrasts shelter with driving away; this denier actively shoves the orphan away (“يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ”). | terra: فَذَٰلِكَ الَّذِي يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ stages an orphan being forcefully repelled; its root is distinct from و د ع, but its action combines the section's driven-away and neglected-orphan images.
luna: The section links the orphan’s neglect to need left uncared for; this neighboring verse condemns failure to urge feeding the poor, completing the actions of the denier in 107:2.
terra: Abu Lahab's wealth does not avail him, using غ ن ي in the “benefit or suffice” sense to deny that possessions can provide lasting security.
